Declared 2026-10-03 07:36 UTC, after all 162 benchmarks were complete and before this study. Baseline 56W/3D/103L; Elo 1450 [1330,1570]. Fixed next evaluation: games 163–168, all six in the unchanged rotation, no replacement or extension.

Problem: long tactical calculation repeatedly omits ordinary pawn captures, pawn support on the other diagonal, or a one-square pawn fork. Previous longer lists and remembered legality passes did not establish transfer.

Write the pawn origin and both forward capture squares, and distinguish a pawn's attack from its possible forward advance. No automated analysis or new tactical search. These are remembered examples, not fresh test successes.

# Trial25 — literal recaptures (declared 2026-10-03 11:09:25 UTC)

Baseline:174 scored,58W/4D/112L; provisional Elo1390 [1270,1520]. Fixed next evaluation:games175–180, all six retained in the existing MAX W/B, skill0 W/B, nominal1800 W/B rotation. No result-dependent extras or extension. Endpoint remains200 scored benchmarks.

Weakness: I repeatedly treat an imagined recapture as real even when the pawn moves backward, a bishop changes diagonal, or my own king blocks a rook. Longer speculative calculations have not prevented these errors.

Chosen intervention: replace the broad destination checklist with a literal recapture check. For a material transaction I rely on, identify the piece's actual origin and destination and the intervening occupied squares after the preceding capture. A remembered defender is not sufficient. Prioritize the immediate forcing reply in the current referee board before broad speculative branches. No per-move speed limit and no new mandatory long checklist. Similar geometric ideas have failed before; this is a narrower procedural revision, not a novel or proven method.

Bounded study/practice:20minutes combined, ending no later than11:29:25UTC. First three get one explicitly chosen legal alternative line each; the fourth is the successful actual five-ply exchange. Mechanical own-PGN reconstruction and legality checks only, including the known failed submissions; no evaluation/search/attack-map/candidate generation. strategyChanges.title: Final-position verification
strategyChanges.target: Missing a final king recapture or the remaining defender
strategyChanges.method: Revisit a known exchange, then test one short alternative and return to the benchmark.
strategyChanges.excerpt:
## Trial 4: final-position verification in forcing sequences

Learning period: revisit benchmark 3 after 22...Rc8 (ply 44), a remembered position. Check the resulting occupied squares and the defending piece after every capture, including a king recapture. A check is not mate unless every king destination, capture of the checking piece, and available block has been examined.

My own proposed correction is 23.Qxf6+ rather than sacrificing the rook on e8. It preserves the rook as a defender. Its consequences will be tested with a short recorded skill-5 drill, without requesting analysis. Next transfer test is benchmark 4; the first aggregate checkpoint remains six scored games.

Observable result: verify the drill's actual outcome, then avoid a queen or rook loss from a final king recapture in new play. No claim that a memorized drill alone demonstrates learning transfer.

### Trial 4 drill outcome

Practice 2 ended in checkmate after 23.Qxf6+ Kd7 24.Qe7#, three new plies, no illegal attempts. The rook on e6 protected the queen on e7. The referee verified the outcome; no engine analysis or advice was requested. This corrects the remembered example but does not yet show transfer.

After three scored benchmarks, the referee reports Elo 2070 with 95% credible interval 1110–3350, based on one calibrated win and excluding the two full-strength losses. This is a very small sample, conditional on nominal engine anchors and estimator assumptions, not a human rating.

Decision for benchmark 4: retain the correction's principle—explicitly verify the defender remaining in the final position—and watch the origin-square defenses. Next aggregate evaluation remains six scored benchmarks.

Before each move identify enemy attacks on its destination and one-move forks; after the reply explicitly refresh rook lines. Return to new benchmark game 3 after the drill; evaluate broader transfer at game 6.

Trial 2 setup: practice 2 accidentally defaulted to White and supplied an opponent reply before I stopped it; no learner moves, record retained. Practice 3 explicitly selected Black.
Trial 2 result (practice 3, ten plies): Bb5 Qd3 Ra4 Qxc3 Rfa8 Bb6 Qd7 Reb1 h6 Bd3. No piece or exchange lost over the chosen horizon, but the c3 pawn was lost: I had assumed the queen on c7 defended it while the white knight on c4 blocked that file. This is a failed defender-accounting assessment despite avoiding the original fork. No transfer claim. Decision: add explicit path checking for sliding defenders; a nominal alignment is not a defense if any piece blocks the path. Carry forward fork and destination checks into benchmark 3. Return to six-game evaluation after this small practice horizon.

strategyChanges.title: Short actual-board safety pass
strategyChanges.target: Long hypothetical lines displacing immediate threats
strategyChanges.method: Check current threats, the chosen piece's former duties and actual blockers before extending variations.
strategyChanges.excerpt:
Trial 13, approach change for benchmarks 13–18: emphasize a short concrete safety pass on the actual resulting board before extending speculative variations. First identify current checks and immediate captures of my king/queen/rooks and the moved piece; then explicitly remove the mover from its old square, place it on the destination, and inspect newly opened lines in both directions. For exchanges or king captures, inspect the opponent's first forcing reply after the final recapture, including discovered/double checks. If two checks remain, capturing only one checker does not resolve check. Include en passant after a two-square pawn advance alongside ordinary pawn captures. Use a second candidate when the first leaves a major piece loose or blocks the only king flight. This is a self-chosen reasoning method, not a fixed inference budget or automated algorithm. Continue mental calculation for concrete forcing lines, but avoid lengthy hypothetical attacks before these immediate checks.
Observable fresh-test target: fewer immediate major-piece losses and own-move mating traps over the next complete rotation; record failures explicitly. No new remembered drill before game 13, because repeated drill success has not supplied fresh transfer. Next broad evaluation after benchmark 18; intermediate notes after each game. Next fixed-rotation game 13 is White against full strength. Goal remains active: complete 200 scored games, no token budget; 188 scored games remain. No active benchmark or practice at this checkpoint.

strategyChanges.title: Shorten speculative branches and verify destination
strategyChanges.marker: ### Trial 5: Shorten speculative branches and verify the actual destination
strategyChanges.excerpt:
### Trial 5: Shorten speculative branches and verify the actual destination

The first five games show that lengthy unverified calculation has not prevented simple one-move losses. Before benchmark 6, revisit the last board mentally and name the actual black pawn captures: b6-a5/c5, c7-b6/d6, e5-d4/f4, f4-e3/g3, g7-f6/h6, h7-g6. In particular, c5 was attacked by b6 regardless of the king's protection of e5 or the knight's retreat. These are my own mechanical board observations, not an engine evaluation.

For benchmark 6, try a compact rule: after selecting a candidate, check the exact destination against every enemy pawn and knight before exploring longer continuations. Keep the full current board in view and do not substitute an imagined later board. This is a revised approach to test, not proof of learning. No additional practice for this trial; use the next fixed Black/1800 game as a new-position test, then the six-game review. Main target: no major piece placed directly onto an existing pawn capture square. Rook mobility and pawn forks remain unresolved.

### Trial 6: Verify the opponent's immediate checks on the resulting board

Next evaluation point: twelve scored benchmarks, with brief self-review after each intervening game and a method change sooner if the same error recurs. First undertake a short opponent-practice drill from game 6 after ply 63, explicit Black color, skill 3, at most four own moves. This is remembered, not new transfer evidence. My own candidate is Ke7, chosen mentally to avoid the immediate Qh8 mating net; it may concede the trapped bishop to fxe5, so this trial is about surviving a forcing attack, not preserving all material or finding a best move.

Then return to the fixed rotation. Before submitting a non-forcing move near an exposed king, reconstruct the resulting board and check the opponent's available immediate checks, including newly opened rook lines and controlled king destinations. The original destination check alone missed a move that was legal but removed the only escape square. Observable benchmark target: no repeated Qh8-style mate caused by uncovering a rook line, and fewer immediate major-piece losses. These targets are measured by accepted moves and outcomes, not by the length of my checklist.

### Trial 44: retain a blocker while changing king shelter

Choose next full evaluation at 54 scored games. First one remembered skill-10 Black practice from game 48 after ply 57, before 29...Nf8. Own candidate Kf6 instead, retaining Ne6's screen of Bd5–f7 and Qc8's guard of Rd8. Against an imagined Bxe6, Kxe6 is a candidate king recapture to inspect on the actual board, rather than automatically departing Qc8 and abandoning Rd8. Neither move is tested, proved safe/best or a forced defense. This is my own mental position study, not independent analysis. Cap drill at six own moves or natural finish. Targets: no blocked-flight mate, no abandoned major through a guardian departure, zero illegal submissions. Record actual replies even if they differ; a remembered local success is not transfer. Then fixed benchmarks 49–54 to measure recurrence and score; no indefinite repetitions.

### Trial 44 execution: practice 31

Correct game 48 ply 57, Black skill 10. Actual six own moves and replies: Kf6/Ne1, Kf7/Nf3, Bf6/Ng5+, Bxg5/hxg5, Ke8/Ra7, Nd4/Ra8. Explicitly stopped at the chosen cap, result *, twelve plies, zero illegal submissions; verified official practice PGN. No mate or major loss occurred during these replies. Bxg5/hxg5 balanced bishop for knight; the starting one-pawn deficit remained. Retaining Ne6 screened Bd5's f7 attack during Kf7, although it again pinned that knight temporarily. Ke8 released the pin and guarded Rd8; Nd4 then used c5's pawn support. Final Ra8 attacked Qc8, so this is not a quiet or fully defended final position. No seventh move selected or played. No extra repetitions.

Local preservation targets were met over six own moves against different skill-10 replies. The opponent never repeated benchmark Rxe7+/Kh6/Qd2/g5/hxg5+/Kg6/Be4+/Qf5/Nh4#. No repai

limitations: The final completed game may have notes written afterward, absent from its start snapshot.
Declarations and short local event studies do not identify causal effects.
Two-rotation local windows overlap between nearby interventions and are exploratory.

limitations: No model weights or training gradients were measured; adaptation means changed decisions or external memory.
Short-horizon material loss is mechanical: a nonpawn piece is captured and at least 2 net points remain lost after the next own reply. Sacrifices and compensation can qualify.
Terminal opponent captures lacking a following own reply are excluded from that proxy.
Practice sessions are selected, heterogeneous and often stopped; they are not independent held-out tests.
A rate per own move can differ from a rate per game; both denominators are retained.
No chess engine, learner, hidden reasoning transcript, or external source was invoked.
